652.title: First Sunday of Lent
652.hook: the gospel is always the temptation in the desert
652.tomorrow: The Chair of Saint Peter (22 February)
652.howItsDone: On the First Sunday of Lent the gospel is always the temptation of Jesus in the desert, and in many dioceses the bishop celebrates the Rite of Election for adults preparing for baptism at Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ash Wednesday: dust, and Joel's line, rend your hearts. Is your quiet sacrifice still a secret? Day six hundred fifty-two.

The Sunday readings change on a three-year cycle. Matthew one year, Mark the next, Luke the third. Most of the gospels change from one year to the next. But on the first Sunday of Lent, whichever year it is, whichever gospel, the story is the same: Jesus, alone in the wilderness, hungry, and tempted. The Church has fixed it there like a signpost at the trailhead. Before you walk the forty days, here's who walked them first, and how it went.
screen: `A THREE-YEAR CYCLE.` → `ONE STORY THAT NEVER MOVES.` → `A SIGNPOST AT THE TRAILHEAD.`

segments.voice: Right after his baptism, the voice from heaven still ringing, the Spirit leads Jesus into the desert. He fasts forty days and forty nights, and afterward, the text says simply, he was hungry. Forty is not a random number. Israel wandered forty years in the wilderness. Moses stayed forty days on the mountain. Elijah walked forty days to the mountain of God. Jesus steps into the same desert his people knew. Then the tempter comes, three times. First, the hungry man: if thou be the Son of God, command that these stones be made bread. He answers from Deuteronomy, in the Douay-Rheims: "Not in bread alone doth man live, but in every word that proceedeth from the mouth of God." Second, on the pinnacle of the temple: throw yourself down, the angels will catch you. Third, on a high mountain, all the kingdoms of the world, his for one act of worship. Each time he answers with a line from Deuteronomy, the book of Israel's own desert years. Three temptations, people have noticed, that touch almost everyone: comfort, attention, and power. Mark tells the whole thing in two verses, and adds a detail no other Gospel has: he was with the wild beasts, and the angels ministered to him. On this Sunday, in many dioceses, adults preparing for baptism at Easter are presented to the bishop and enrolled, the Rite of Election. Their forty days begin with his. Lent, in Latin, is Quadragesima, the fortieth. The whole season is shaped like this desert.
screen: `LED INTO THE DESERT.` · `FORTY, THE OLD NUMBER.` · `BREAD, A LEAP, THE KINGDOMS.` · `COMFORT, ATTENTION, POWER.` · then, large: `NOT IN BREAD ALONE DOTH MAN LIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your desert. Sit, and let it get quiet. Ask what your wilderness is right now: a loneliness, a waiting, a craving, a fear, a stretch of life where things feel empty. Name it plainly, in one word if you can. Then ask which of the three pulls at you hardest there: comfort, attention, or power. No judging. Just naming. If you pray, you can ask for the angels Mark mentions, to minister to you. If you don't, simply stay with what you named. The bell holds the time.
First Sunday of Lent. The Sunday when the gospel, every year, is Jesus tempted in the desert for forty days. Today's word.
Your line: forty days. Today, when one of the three pulls at you, comfort, attention or power, notice it and name it. Day six hundred fifty-two.

screen: `DAY 652 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE CHAIR OF SAINT PETER.`

653.title: The Chair of Saint Peter (22 February)
653.hook: a feast of Peter's teaching office, not a piece of furniture
653.howItsDone: Catholics keep February 22 as the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter, praying for the pope; in Saint Peter's Basilica the altar of the Chair is decorated with candles for the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the First Sunday of Lent: the desert, three temptations, and your line, forty days. Which pull did you notice: comfort, attention or power? Day six hundred fifty-three.

Walk to the far end of Saint Peter's Basilica in Rome, past the great canopy over the altar, and look up. Floating in a burst of gilded rays, held up by four giant bronze figures, is a chair. A huge, ornate bronze throne by the sculptor Bernini. Tourists photograph it and ask, is that where the pope sits? It isn't. And the feast on February 22 isn't really about a chair either. It's about a word that gave us cathedral.
screen: `THE FAR END OF SAINT PETER'S.` → `A FLOATING BRONZE CHAIR.` → `NOT WHERE THE POPE SITS.`

segments.voice: In the ancient world, a teacher sat to teach. The chair, in Greek and Latin cathedra, was the sign of authority to teach. A bishop's church is called a cathedral because his chair is in it. So the Chair of Saint Peter is a feast of a role, not of furniture: Peter's office of teaching and holding the Church together, which Catholics believe continues in the bishop of Rome. The gospel is Matthew 16. Jesus asks his disciples, who do people say I am? Then, who do you say I am? Simon answers: Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God. And Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "That thou art Peter; and upon this rock I will build my church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it." It's a pun. Peter's new name, Petros in Greek, Kepha in Aramaic, means rock. Christians read this verse differently, and fairly. Catholics see here Peter's office as the rock, handed on to his successors. Orthodox Christians honor Peter as first among the apostles but understand that primacy differently. Many Protestants read the rock as Peter's confession of faith, or as Christ himself. Inside Bernini's bronze chair is an older wooden one, long honored as Peter's; scholars date it to the ninth century. The Church once kept two separate feasts of Peter's chair, one for Rome and one for Antioch, where tradition says he led the church first; they were combined on this day. And remember who got the name: the same man who would deny knowing Jesus three times. The rock was a man who cracked, and was forgiven.
screen: `A TEACHER SAT TO TEACH.` · `WHO DO YOU SAY I AM?` · `PETROS, KEPHA: ROCK.` · `ONE VERSE, READ DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `UPON THIS ROCK I WILL BUILD MY CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold someone who carries a heavy responsibility. Catholics pray for the pope today, and if you pray, you can do that: for his health, his judgment, his peace. If you don't, choose anyone who has to hold a group together: a parent, a principal, a team lead, a pastor. Sit with what it must be like to be the rock others lean on, and to be a person who can crack. Wish them strength. The bell holds the time.
The Chair of Saint Peter. A feast on February 22 of Peter's office of teaching and unity, which Catholics believe continues in the pope. Today's word.
screen: `THE CHAIR OF SAINT PETER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: upon this rock. Today, be steady for one person who's leaning on you, even if you've cracked before. Day six hundred fifty-three.

654.title: Saint Patrick (17 March)
654.hook: the breastplate prayer: Christ before me, Christ behind me
654.howItsDone: Catholics keep March 17 as the feast of Saint Patrick, a solemnity and holy day in Ireland; many go to Mass before the parades, and the Breastplate prayer is often sung as a hymn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Chair of Saint Peter: a teacher's chair, a pun on rock, and your line, upon this rock. Who leaned on you, and did you hold? Day six hundred fifty-four.

Green rivers, green beer, plastic hats, a parade down Fifth Avenue. On March 17, half the world becomes a little bit Irish. Ask anyone at the parade who Saint Patrick was and you'll hear: he drove the snakes out of Ireland and explained the Trinity with a shamrock. Both stories are much later legends. Ireland, as far as scientists can tell, had no snakes after the Ice Age. The real Patrick left us something better than legends: his own words, and a prayer that carries his name.
screen: `GREEN RIVERS, GREEN BEER.` → `SNAKES AND SHAMROCKS.` → `HIS OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Patrick wasn't Irish. He was born in Roman Britain in the fifth century, the son of a deacon, a boy who by his own account didn't take faith very seriously. At about sixteen, raiders from Ireland seized him and sold him as a slave. For six years he herded animals on a cold hillside, and there, alone, he began to pray, he says, a hundred times a day and almost as many at night. Then he escaped, found a ship, and made it home. And years later, he went back. Back to the land of the people who had enslaved him, as a bishop, to spend his life among them. We know this because he wrote it down, in a short Latin work called the Confession, which opens with Patrick calling himself a sinner and very unlearned. It's one of the very few documents we have from Britain or Ireland in that century. Then there's the prayer. It's called the Breastplate, or the Deer's Cry, and tradition says Patrick sang it while walking past enemies who wanted him dead. Most scholars think it was written later, maybe two or three centuries after him, in Old Irish, and attributed to him. Either way, it's a prayer of armor. It calls on the Trinity, then the strength of heaven, sun, fire, sea and rock. Then the famous part: Christ with me, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ in me, beneath me, above me. And it ends looking outward, asking for Christ in the heart of everyone who thinks of me, and in every eye that sees me. A prayer that surrounds you, and then sees Christ in the faces around you.
screen: `A BRITISH BOY, ENSLAVED.` · `HE WENT BACK.` · `THE CONFESSION, IN LATIN.` · `THE BREASTPLATE, LATER.` · then, large: `CHRIST IN EVERY EYE THAT SEES ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the breastplate surround you. Sit, and breathe slowly. Then, with each breath, notice one direction: in front of you, behind you, to your right, to your left, below you, above you. If you pray, you can pray those old lines, Christ before me, Christ behind me, Christ beside me, one direction at a time. If you don't, simply feel the space around you and the people you'll meet today. Then think of the eyes that will see you, and the eyes you'll see. The bell holds the time.
Saint Patrick. A fifth-century Briton, once enslaved in Ireland, who returned as its bishop; patron of Ireland, kept on March 17. Today's word.
Your line: christ in every eye. Today, look at three people's faces, really look, and see what the breastplate saw. Day six hundred fifty-four.

655.title: Saint Joseph (19 March)
655.hook: the silent guardian, patron of the universal Church and workers
655.howItsDone: Catholics keep March 19 as the Solemnity of Saint Joseph, Spouse of the Blessed Virgin Mary; in Sicily and in Italian-American communities families set a Saint Joseph's table and share the food with the poor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saint Patrick, the enslaved boy who went back. Your line was christ in every eye. Whose face did you really look at? Day six hundred fifty-five.

Go through all four Gospels with a highlighter and mark every word Joseph says. You'll finish with a clean highlighter. Not one word. Mary speaks. The shepherds speak. Even the innkeeper is implied. Joseph, the man who raised Jesus, taught him a trade, carried him to Egypt and back, never says anything the Gospels record. And yet the Church has made him patron of the whole Catholic Church. Two days after Patrick's parade, the quietest man in the story gets a solemnity.
screen: `A CLEAN HIGHLIGHTER.` → `NOT ONE WORD.` → `PATRON OF THE WHOLE CHURCH.`

segments.voice: Matthew introduces him in a crisis. Joseph is betrothed to Mary, and she turns out to be pregnant, and not by him. Under the custom of the time he could have shamed her publicly. Instead, in the Douay-Rheims, Joseph, "being a just man, and not willing publicly to expose her, was minded to put her away privately." Just, here, means right with God, and his justice comes out as mercy. Then an angel speaks to him in a dream: do not be afraid to take Mary your wife. And Matthew records what he does: "And Joseph rising up from sleep, did as the angel of the Lord had commanded him, and took unto him his wife." That's the pattern of his whole story. Four times in Matthew, Joseph is told something in a dream, and every time, he gets up and does it. Takes Mary home. Flees to Egypt by night. Comes back. Settles in Nazareth. No speeches. Obedience and work. Mark's Gospel calls Jesus the carpenter, and Matthew calls him the carpenter's son, so Joseph worked with his hands and passed the trade on. The Gospels never mention his death. Tradition says he died before Jesus began preaching, with Jesus and Mary beside him, which is why Catholics call him patron of a happy death. In 1870 Pope Pius IX named him patron of the universal Church: the man who guarded the Holy Family now guards the larger family. In 1955 Pius XII added a second feast, Saint Joseph the Worker, on May 1. And in Sicily, families still set a Saint Joseph's table today, loaded with bread and sweets, and give it to the poor.
screen: `A JUST MAN, AND MERCIFUL.` · `HE ROSE AND DID IT.` · `FOUR DREAMS, NO SPEECHES.` · `GUARDIAN OF THE WHOLE CHURCH.` · then, large: `THE SILENT SAINT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do your work well, quietly. Sit, and think of the work in front of you today, paid or unpaid: a report, a shift, a meal, a lesson, a repair. Choose one task, and decide to do it carefully, without needing anyone to notice or thank you. Picture yourself doing it the way a good carpenter planes a board: slow, attentive, finished properly. If you pray, you can ask Saint Joseph to work alongside you. If you don't, simply commit to the task. The bell holds the time.
Saint Joseph. Husband of Mary and guardian of Jesus, who says nothing in the Gospels; patron of the universal Church, kept on March 19. Today's word.
Your line: the silent saint. Today, do one good thing without saying a word about it. Day six hundred fifty-five.

656.title: The Annunciation (25 March)
656.hook: nine months before Christmas, the Word takes flesh
656.howItsDone: Catholics keep March 25 as the Solemnity of the Annunciation of the Lord (moved when it falls in Holy Week or the Easter octave), kneel at the Creed's words on the incarnation, and many pray the Angelus at 6 a.m., noon and 6 p.m.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saint Joseph, who never says a word in the Gospels. Your line was the silent saint. What good thing did you do without mentioning it? Day six hundred fifty-six.

Count back nine months from December 25. You land on March 25. The Church did that math centuries ago, and so in the middle of Lent, with purple on the altar and Easter still weeks off, there's a sudden white solemnity. Christmas, seen from the beginning. In old Europe, bells in villages rang three times a day, at dawn, at noon and at dusk, and farmers in the fields stopped and bowed their heads to remember this exact moment. Some churches still ring them. Today, the moment the bells remember.
screen: `NINE MONTHS BEFORE CHRISTMAS.` → `WHITE IN THE MIDDLE OF LENT.` → `BELLS AT DAWN, NOON, DUSK.`

segments.voice: Luke sets it in Nazareth, a village nobody expected anything from. The angel Gabriel comes to a young woman, betrothed to Joseph, and greets her: hail, full of grace. He tells her she will conceive a son, and call him Jesus, and he will be called the Son of the Most High. Mary doesn't simply nod. She asks a real question, in the Douay-Rheims: "How shall this be done, because I know not man?" The angel answers that the Holy Spirit will come upon her, and the power of the Most High will overshadow her. He tells her that her old cousin Elizabeth, called barren, is six months pregnant. "Because no word shall be impossible with God." And then Mary's answer, the hinge of the whole story: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it done to me according to thy word." In Latin, the first word of that last phrase is fiat, let it be done. Catholics often call this Mary's fiat. It's not passive. She asked, she listened, and she chose. Christians believe that in that moment the Word, who in John's gospel was there in the beginning, took flesh in her. That's why, at Mass today, people kneel at the words of the Creed about the incarnation, just as they do on Christmas. And that's what the bells were for. The Angelus, rung morning, noon and evening, walks through this scene in three short lines with a Hail Mary after each: the angel's message, Mary's be it done, and the Word made flesh. A whole Christmas, three times a day, in less than two minutes.
screen: `GABRIEL IN NAZARETH.` · `HOW SHALL THIS BE DONE?` · `NO WORD IMPOSSIBLE WITH GOD.` · `FIAT: LET IT BE DONE.` · then, large: `BE IT DONE TO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the Angelus, or its shape. If you pray and know it, pray the Angelus now: the three short verses, each followed by a Hail Mary. If you don't know it, let its shape guide the sit. First breath, a message arrives. Second breath, a question is asked. Third breath, a yes is given. Then sit with something you've been asked to carry that you didn't plan. A job, a person, a change. Hold it, and ask whether a yes is possible. The bell holds the time.
The Annunciation. The angel Gabriel's message to Mary, and her yes, kept on March 25, nine months before Christmas. Today's word.
Your line: be it done. Today, at noon, wherever you are, stop for ten seconds and remember the moment in Nazareth. Day six hundred fifty-six.

657.title: Laetare Sunday
657.hook: the rose vestments again, halfway through Lent
657.howItsDone: On the fourth Sunday of Lent the priest may wear rose vestments instead of violet, and the entrance antiphon begins with Isaiah 66:10, Laetare, Jerusalem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Annunciation: a question, an answer, and your line, be it done. Did you stop at noon and remember Nazareth? Day six hundred fifty-seven.

Anyone who has run a long race knows the halfway marker. Your legs hurt, your enthusiasm from the start line is gone, and the finish is still a long way off. Then a sign, a water table, someone on the curb cheering, and you find a little more. Lent has one too. On its fourth Sunday, for one day, the violet gives way to rose. If you were with us back in Advent on Gaudete Sunday, you've seen this color before. It shows up only twice a year, and both times it means the same thing.

Laetare is Latin for rejoice, said to one: to a city. It's the first word of the old entrance chant for the fourth Sunday of Lent, from the last chapter of Isaiah. In the Douay-Rheims: "Rejoice with Jerusalem, and be glad with her, all you that love her." Isaiah wrote to people who had mourned Jerusalem's ruin, promising that the city would be like a mother again, nursing and comforting her children. The Church picked that verse for the middle of Lent, when the fasting starts to feel long, the resolutions are wobbling, and Easter is still out of sight. So for one day, the color lightens. Flowers, which are usually left off the altar in Lent, may come back. The organ, often quieter in Lent, can play more freely. It's sometimes called Mid-Lent Sunday, and in England and Ireland it's also Mothering Sunday, a day people once traveled to their mother church, the cathedral or the parish of their baptism, and which later became a day to honor mothers too. In some years, the gospel is the prodigal son, the story with a feast for the one who came home. In others it's the man born blind, who sees. Both are stories where the long darkness breaks. Rome kept a custom too: on this Sunday popes would bless a golden rose, an ornament of gold sometimes given to a church or a person as an honor. Gaudete in Advent, Laetare in Lent. One comes in the dark of December, one as Lent's fasting starts to drag, and each time the color tells the people in the pews how far they've already come.
screen: `LAETARE: REJOICE, O CITY.` · `JERUSALEM LIKE A MOTHER.` · `FLOWERS AND ORGAN RETURN.` · `GAUDETE AND LAETARE.` · then, large: `REJOICE WITH JERUSALEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take a breath of joy. Sit, and breathe in slowly, as though you're breathing in something good: fresh air, morning, coffee, the smell of rain. Hold it a moment. Breathe out whatever has felt heavy this Lent, or this month. Do that a few times. Then name one thing you're honestly glad about today, however small. Let it be enough. If you pray, you can say Isaiah's word, rejoice. If you don't, just let the gladness have a minute. The bell holds the time.
Laetare. Latin for rejoice; the fourth Sunday of Lent, halfway to Easter, with rose vestments. Today's word.
Your line: halfway, rejoice. Today, if you're in the middle of something long, celebrate the halfway point out loud. Day six hundred fifty-seven.

658.title: Palm Sunday
658.hook: the palms and the long passion read with the whole congregation
658.howItsDone: On Palm Sunday of the Passion of the Lord, Catholics receive blessed palms, process into church, and hear the Passion read, often in parts with the congregation reading the crowd; many keep the palms at home until next year's Ash Wednesday.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Laetare, the rose halfway through Lent. Your line was halfway, rejoice. What did you celebrate in the middle of something long? Day six hundred fifty-eight.

It's the one Sunday you leave Mass holding a plant. Ushers hand out strips of palm at the door, and kids immediately start sword fighting with them, or folding them into crosses. The service begins outside, or at the back, with a procession and singing. Everyone is waving branches. It feels like a parade. Then, twenty minutes later, the same congregation, holding the same palms, will be reading aloud a line nobody wants to say. Palm Sunday is the only Sunday that turns around in the middle.
screen: `A PLANT AT THE DOOR.` → `A PARADE WITH BRANCHES.` → `THE SUNDAY THAT TURNS AROUND.`

segments.voice: First, the entry. Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a donkey, a king's entrance done humbly, as the prophet Zechariah had pictured. People throw their cloaks and branches on the road and shout, in Matthew's account, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord: Hosanna in the highest." Hosanna is Hebrew, from Psalm 118: save, please. A cry for rescue that had become a shout of welcome. The palms are blessed and the people process, re-enacting it. Then the Mass begins, and the gospel is the Passion, the whole account of his arrest, trial and death, from Matthew, Mark or Luke depending on the year. It's long, and in many parishes it's read in parts. A reader narrates. The priest takes the words of Jesus. And the congregation reads the crowd. So the same voices that sang hosanna at the door find themselves saying, together, crucify him. That's deliberate. The Church isn't pointing at a crowd two thousand years ago and saying, look what they did. It's handing the line to everyone in the pews. Catholic teaching is clear that the blame for his death falls on all sinners, not on any one people. Hosanna, then crucify: the same mouths, the same week. People take the palms home and tuck them behind a crucifix or a picture, and next year, they're burned to make the ashes for Ash Wednesday. And this week behind us: forty days, upon this rock, christ in every eye, the silent saint, be it done, halfway, rejoice. Now the week everything has pointed toward.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep a palm at home. If you have one from church, find a place for it: behind a crucifix, over a door, tucked into a picture frame. If you don't, find any green leaf or small branch and set it somewhere you'll see it this week. Sit with it. Think about how quickly cheering can turn, in a crowd, in a friendship, in yourself. If you pray, you can say the old cry, hosanna, save, please. If you don't, simply hold the leaf and the week ahead. The bell holds the time.
Palm Sunday. The Sunday before Easter: palms and a procession, then the Passion read aloud, with the congregation as the crowd. Today's word.
Your line: hosanna, then crucify. Today, notice when you're about to turn on someone you praised, and stop. Day six hundred fifty-eight.

fork.reveal: the congregation reads the crowd: crucify him. the same voices that sang hosanna at the door. the Church hands the line to everyone.

original.note: Hebrew: save, please, from Psalm 118:25; the root of hosanna.

trapdoor: what you thought: Palm Sunday is a happy parade before Easter.
what it means: the day turns from hosanna at the door to crucify in the Passion, and the congregation says both.
what a scholar hears: hosanna is Hebrew hoshia na from Psalm 118:25; the entry echoes Zechariah 9:9; reading the Passion in parts places the guilt on all, not one people.
